title: From denial to exploitation: how the Kremlin has adapted its climate disinformation
content:
In the latest wave of climate-related narratives spread by the Kremlin, climate change is a vehicle to reinforce familiar disinformation tropes: the alleged authoritarianism and hypocrisy of the EU, Europe’s supposed self-inflicted decline through sanctions against Russia, and, ultimately, the claim that Europe has no choice but to restore relations with Russia as a supplier of affordable oil and gas.

Climate change used to be a fringe topic in Kremlin propaganda. It was rarely mentioned, and when it was, it was often accompanied by absurd claims or outright denial. But as the effects of climate change become increasingly difficult to ignore (including domestically in Russia), pro-Kremlin outlets have largely stopped denying its existence. Instead, they have woven it into their disinformation ecosystem, shifting from denying the problem to discrediting proposed solutions.

title: From social media to the front line: Russia’s foreign recruitment pipeline
content: This report traces how Russia sustains its war in Ukraine by recruiting foreign nationals, many of them deceived or coerced, through a global pipeline of social media advertisements, intermediaries and disposable websites. It centres on a recent investigation by the European External Action Service (EEAS), which uncovered a coordinated digital infrastructure behind this recruitment drive.

title: My home is not my castle: Kaliningrad as an address for Kremlin propaganda. Part 2
content:
In official discourse, Kaliningrad is increasingly portrayed as Russia’s western fortress: resilient, patriotic, and under constant external pressure. Yet propaganda must also compete with people’s everyday experience. Rising prices, logistical disruption, security alerts and the militarisation of public life shape how residents perceive the consequences of Russia’s war. This article examines that tension between official narratives and lived reality.

The weakest point of Kremlin propaganda in Kaliningrad Oblast is the collision between the official picture of the world and the everyday economy. A person may repeat familiar formulas about ‘unfriendly countries’, ‘sanctions pressure’, and the ‘threat from the West’, while at the same time seeing that the ordinary food basket is becoming more expensive, familiar goods periodically disappear, and the region is increasingly dependent on complicated and costly logistics. In Kaliningrad, the war is felt through the price tag.

title: My home is not my castle: Kaliningrad as an address for Kremlin propaganda. Part 1
content:
Kaliningrad Oblast is a Russian semi-exclave on the Baltic Sea, separated from mainland Russia and located between Lithuania and Poland – both members of the EU and NATO. The region itself was created after the Second World War from the northern part of former East Prussia, transferred to the USSR under the Potsdam agreements in 1945. This makes Kaliningrad simultaneously a Russian territory, a former German space, a Baltic region, and Moscow’s military outpost on the border with the European Union.

Unlike most Russian regions, Kaliningrad for a long time lived not simply in a Russian reality, but in a European borderland everyday life. The local border traffic agreement between Poland and Kaliningrad Oblast significantly increased cross-border mobility. Even after it was suspended in 2016, the memory of that openness remained an important part of local identity. For Kaliningraders, Europe was not an abstract ‘hostile West’ from television, but a nearby and recognisable space just a few kilometres away.

title: Why the information space has become a minefield for EU CSDP missions and operations
content:
When Armenian voters renewed Prime Minister Nikol Pashinyan’s mandate in the June 2026 parliamentary elections, they did more than choose a government. They chose closer cooperation with the European Union. That choice made them a target.

As Armenia deepened its relations with the EU, it became a frequent target of Russian Foreign Information Manipulation and Interference (FIMI). Attempts to discredit European engagements are a recurring feature relayed across social media platforms, inauthentic news websites, and foreign state-controlled outlets. FIMI has specifically targeted the EU mission in Armenia (EUMA), which was established in 2023 to monitor and support confidence-building in conflict-affected areas in the country. This pattern is telling: modern influence operations do not happen only during war time. They seek to divide partners, distort facts, shape people’s minds, manipulate their emotions, and influence their decisions.

title: Russia’s attacks on Ukraine’s cultural heritage: a nail in the coffin of FIMI
content:
The Kyiv Pechersk Lavra, a sacred site that the Kremlin has for decades called its spiritual cradle and a main centre for Orthodoxy in Russia, is now in the crosshairs of Russian weapons. On the night of 15 June 2026, Russia launched a missile and drone strike on Kyiv that caused a massive fire in the Dormition Cathedral of the Lavra. Ukrainian authorities have estimated the damage to the ancient shrine, one of eight UNESCO World Heritage sites, at over 500 million hryvnias (about 10 million euros). Restoration and reconstruction work could take two years.

The strike was not just an attack on Ukrainian cultural heritage. It also destroyed a principal historical narrative of pro-Russian Foreign Information Manipulation and Interference (FIMI) that portrays Moscow as the protector of the Orthodox Church.

title: Russia’s information war against Ukraine’s European future is a threat to Europe itself
content:
Ukraine’s accession to the European Union is not only a political process. It is a strategic security choice for Ukraine and for Europe. That is why Russia is attacking it not only with missiles, but also with manipulation, fear, and distrust.

A joint report by the European External Action Service (EEAS) and the Center for Countering Disinformation (CCD), Beyond the Battlefield: Russia’s Information War Against Ukraine’s European Future, shows that Russia’s attempts to undermine Ukraine’s EU path are systematic, coordinated, and persistent. They are not isolated ‘fake news’ stories. They are part of a wider Foreign Information Manipulation and Interference (FIMI) ecosystem designed to weaken Ukraine, divide European societies, and damage confidence in enlargement.

title: Explosives and propaganda: Russia’s dual-use drones
content:
Russian First Person View (FPV) drones have become a defining feature of the war in Ukraine. The same drones used to drop explosives on civilians and military targets are also being used to distribute propaganda leaflets in frontline communities, combining physical violence with psychological warfare.

A video report from Kherson

The combination of violence and persuasion may seem contradictory, but studies of coercive control offer an explanation. The Russian tactics in Kherson and other frontline territories of Ukraine follow three conditions for brainwashing described by psychiatrist Robert Jay Lifton in Thought Reform and the Psychology of Totalism.

First comes physical pressure: artillery, FPV drones, and attacks on infrastructure create constant danger and exhaustion. Next comes information disruption: telecommunications collapse or are restricted while propaganda channels fill the vacuum. And finally comes the conditional rescue message: drone-dropped leaflets or Telegram contacts offering safety or assistance to those willing to accept the occupier’s version of reality.

title: How Moscow tries to cover up its failures on the Ukrainian battlefield
content:
Since launching its illegal invasion against Ukraine, Russia has developed a category of narratives aimed at covering the war according to its preferences. However, Russia’s Foreign Information Manipulation and Interference (FIMI) campaign has recently abandoned even the slightest pretence of credibility. While the Ukrainian military is regaining a tactical military advantage and Russian successes on the battlefield are dwindling, Moscow’s disinformation machine is trying to meet the need to show off military victories to its public opinion and partners, even if they are widely exaggerated.

For the first time since 2023, Ukraine is recapturing more territory than it is losing. This was particularly evident in May 2026, when the Russian army managed to occupy only 14 square kilometres in Ukraine, according to open-source intelligence (OSINT) analysts. The number of Russian assaults on Ukrainian positions increased by 37.5%, but this activity did not lead to any significant advances.

title: New EEAS-CCD report exposes Russian FIMI targeting Ukraine’s EU future
content:
Today, the European External Action Service (EEAS) and Ukraine’s Centre for Countering Disinformation (CCD) are publishing a joint analytical report examining how Russian Foreign Information Manipulation and Interference (FIMI) targets Ukraine’s path towards European Union membership.

The report documents a coordinated effort to undermine support for Ukraine’s accession among both Ukrainian and European audiences. While the narratives vary depending on the target audience, their strategic objective is to weaken political and public support for Ukraine’s European future.

Ukraine’s European integration has become one of the Kremlin’s key information targets since the country was granted EU candidate status in June 2022 and accession negotiations formally opened in June 2024. The accession process has become a focal point for discussions about security, reconstruction, economic modernisation, and Ukraine’s long-term geopolitical orientation. As a result, it has also become a prime target for manipulation.
